rawContent: I am looking forward to my talk on Thursday. It’s a sneak peek at the forthcoming (2023-24) new book that @amandanelledgar and I wrote, “The Summer of 2020: George Floyd and the Resurgence of #BlackLivesMatter with @upmiss. https://t.co/Jneo6rmaNE
In the beginning, many people saw #BlackLivesMatter more as a secular movement than a spiritual one. However, this anti-religious narrative surrounding BLM was not entirely true.

Many are beginning to argue that BLM, since its inception, was and has always been a spiritual movement. For instance, #BLM Black-LA co-founder @DocMellyMel argues that despite people framing BLM as a secular movement, there has always been a component of spirituality in #BLM.

@BikoMandelaGray argues that #BLM has “religious undertones through its celebration of Black life as sacred.” He suggests that “BLM offers a vision of Blackness as irreducibly sacred, as Blackness disrupts the normative significance of the contemporary world”

@ccamrun2 and Philip Luke Sinitiere remind us in their book "Race, Religion, and #BlackLivesMatter: "that “contrary to general perceptions” of #BLM, “religion has been neither absent nor excluded from the movement’s activities.”  https://t.co/awMIRu6F8m

I would agree with their assessment of #BLM and religion because @amandanelledgar and I found similar findings in our book "The Struggle Over Black Lives Matter and All Lives Matter." https://t.co/5JdLdNJi0R

I will share more later, but let me just say, I had a wonderful time with students and faculty with @UTKEnglish! They treated me like I was somebody and it was good to talk about religious rhetoric, social movements, and #BLM. Thanks to Dr. Jeff Ringer for the invite! https://t.co/djWf0xdS3a
